title: Leftovers in Long Division
goal: I can do long division with a remainder, make sure the remainder is smaller than the divisor, and check my answer.

card.desc: Bailey learns long division with remainders on Zoom. She shares 97 cents on 4 plates to see the leftover, learns that the remainder must be smaller than the divisor, and checks with quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend. Seven new words, including maximum and stubborn.

win: You found every leftover, kept it smaller than the divisor, and checked it!

slides.title: Leftovers in Long Division
slides.text: Last week every long division came out even. Today some do not. You will find the remainder, make sure it is not too big, and check your answer by multiplying and adding.

notes.do: Share your screen. Before you start, check that Bailey has at her table: 9 dimes and about 40 pennies (or paper strips and beans), 6 paper plates, paper and a pencil, her book. Keep your whiteboard on camera with the four steps on it.
notes.say: "You already know every step of long division. Today there is one new thing at the very end: what is left over. That's it."
notes.ask: "What is 50 ÷ 8?" (6 R 2.) "You did leftovers with facts in Lesson 10. Today they show up in long division."

slides.title: Back to Berk
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: Tell what happened in the part you read this weekend.
Find a moment when Toothless is stubborn. What does Hiccup do about it?
Does Hiccup give up when things go wrong? Prove it with an event.
starters: Hiccup does / does not give up. For example, …

notes.do: 6 minutes. Let her hold the book up to the camera and read a line.
notes.ask: "What does Hiccup do when Toothless will not listen?"
notes.listen: A real moment from the book and Hiccup's response. Connect it: "When a problem is stubborn, you don't quit; you try one step at a time."

slides.title: Facts you will need today
slides.text: Say the answer out loud. Jonathan types it.

items.no: 4 × 5 = 20 is too big.
Count up from 16 to 17.

items.q: 45 ÷ 7 = ____   (use R for the remainder)
items.no: 7 × 6 = 42. How many are left?

notes.do: She says each answer; you type it.
notes.say: Praise each one: "Yes! That is a step from today's first problem."
notes.listen: The first two are exactly the last step of 97 ÷ 4. The third is the Lesson 10 idea she will need.

slides.title: Words for today
slides.text: Read each card out loud. Then use the word in your own sentence.

words.meaning: What remains after the rest is used or shared. In division, it is the remainder.
words.example: 97 cents on 4 plates: 24 cents each, and 1 cent is the leftover.
The remainder can never equal or exceed the divisor.

words.meaning: The greatest that is possible or allowed.
words.example: When you divide by 6, the maximum remainder is 5.

words.meaning: To change something to make it correct or better.
words.example: My remainder was too big, so I revised my answer: one more group fit.

words.meaning: A small part that is left over from something bigger.
words.example: Only a remnant of the fish pile was left after the dragons ate.

words.meaning: Not willing to change your mind or do what others want.
words.example: Toothless is stubborn: he often refuses to do what Hiccup asks.
We packed ample snacks, so nobody was hungry on the long trip.

notes.do: Flip one card at a time. She reads each one and makes her own sentence. Write remainder < divisor on your whiteboard and keep it on camera.
notes.say: "Leftover, remnant, exceed, maximum and revise are all about remainders. Stubborn and ample are for the book and for life."
notes.ask: "What is the maximum number of cookies you could have left if you share with 5 friends equally?" (4.) "When is Toothless stubborn?"

slides.title: When it does not come out even
slides.text: Share 97 cents on 4 plates: 9 dimes and 7 pennies.

steps.text: Share the dimes: 9 dimes on 4 plates. Each plate gets 2 dimes. 1 dime is left.
Trade that dime for 10 pennies. Now there are 10 + 7 = 17 pennies.
Share 17 pennies on 4 plates: 4 each. 1 penny is left, and it cannot be shared.
Each plate has 24 cents, and 1 cent is left over: 97 ÷ 4 = 24 R 1.

slides.tip: The leftover is the remainder. It is too small to give every plate one more.

notes.do: Hands-on at home: she does each step with her coins on 4 plates before you reveal it.
notes.say: Praise each step: "2 dimes each, yes!" "17 pennies, yes!"
notes.ask: "Why can't we share the last penny?" (4 plates, 1 penny: not enough for everyone.)
notes.listen: She sees the remainder is what can't be shared equally.

slides.title: 97 ÷ 4: the tens
slides.text: Now the same thing with long division. One step at a time.

steps.text: Divide. How many 4s fit in 9? 2 (4 × 2 = 8; 4 × 3 = 12 is too big). Write 2 above the 9 in the tens place.
Multiply. 2 × 4 = 8. Write 8 under the 9.
Subtract. 9 − 8 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 4.

notes.do: She says each step and number before you click. She writes it on paper.
notes.say: Praise each correct step out loud: "Divide, 2. Yes!" "Multiply, 8. Yes!" "1 left, smaller than 4. Perfect."
notes.ask: "Where are those 2 dimes on your plates?" (2 tens each.)

slides.title: 97 ÷ 4: the ones
slides.text: Bring down, divide, multiply, subtract. Then look at what is left.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 7 from the ones place. Now you have 17.
Divide. How many 4s fit in 17? 4 (4 × 4 = 16; 4 × 5 = 20 is too big). Write 4 above the 7 in the ones place.
Multiply. 4 × 4 = 16. Write 16 under the 17.
Subtract. 17 − 16 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 4. There are no more digits to bring down, so 97 ÷ 4 = 24 R 1.
Check: 24 × 4 = 96, and 96 + 1 = 97. It matches the dividend.

notes.say: "Nothing left to bring down, and 1 is smaller than 4. That 1 is the remainder. We write R 1." Praise each step.
notes.listen: "There are no more digits, so the 1 is the remainder."

slides.title: Check it: multiply, then add
slides.text: To check a division with a remainder, multiply the quotient by the divisor. Then add the remainder. You should get the dividend.
slides.tip: Forgetting to add the remainder is the most common slip when checking.

notes.do: Write the rule on your whiteboard under remainder < divisor.
notes.ask: "Why do we add the remainder back?" (Those cents were left in your hand. They are still part of the 97.)
notes.listen: She says the rule in her own words.

slides.title: The remainder rule
slides.text: The remainder must always be smaller than the divisor. If it is not, one more group fits, and you need to revise.

steps.text: Dividing by 7? The remainder can be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. The maximum is 6.
Snotlout wrote 59 ÷ 7 = 7 R 10. 10 exceeds 7, so one more 7 fits.

slides.tip: Check the remainder after EVERY subtraction, not just the last one.

notes.ask: "What is the maximum remainder when you divide by 9?" (8.) "By 2?" (1.)
notes.listen: Maximum remainder = divisor − 1. If she says 9 for ÷ 9, ask: "With 9 left, could you make one more group of 9?"

slides.title: Too big?
slides.text: Say the answer out loud. Jonathan types or taps it.

items.q: When you divide by 6, what is the biggest remainder you can ever have?
items.why: The remainder must be smaller than the divisor, so the maximum remainder for ÷ 6 is 5. A remainder of 6 would make one more group.
items.no: It must be smaller than 6.

items.q: Every answer below checks out when you multiply back. Which one can not be right?
items.why: In 38 ÷ 5 = 6 R 8, the remainder 8 is not smaller than 5, so another group fits. Revise it: 38 ÷ 5 = 7 R 3.
no: 1 is smaller than 4, so this remainder is allowed. Check: 11 × 4 + 1 = 45.
2 is smaller than 6, so this remainder is allowed. Check: 8 × 6 + 2 = 50.
2 is smaller than 3, so this remainder is allowed. Check: 9 × 3 + 2 = 29.

items.why: 13 × 5 = 65, and 65 + 2 = 67. It matches the dividend, so the answer is right.
items.no: Multiply 13 × 5 first. Then add the remainder 2.

notes.do: She answers out loud; you type or tap.
notes.ask: For the second one: "How did you spot it without dividing?" (8 is bigger than 5.)
notes.listen: Check: 13 × 5 = 65, plus 2 = 67. If she says 65, point to the whiteboard rule: add the remainder.

slides.title: 853 ÷ 6: the hundreds
slides.text: Now 3 digits. Same steps.

steps.text: Divide. How many 6s fit in 8? 1 (6 × 1 = 6; 6 × 2 = 12 is too big). Write 1 above the 8 in the hundreds place.
Multiply. 1 × 6 = 6. Write 6 under the 8.
Subtract. 8 − 6 = 2. Check: 2 is smaller than 6.

notes.do: She says each step before you click and writes it on paper.
notes.ask: "Estimate: 6 × 100 = 600 and 6 × 200 = 1,200. So the answer is between…?" (100 and 200.)

slides.title: 853 ÷ 6: the tens
slides.text: Bring down, then the same steps.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 5 from the tens place. Now you have 25.
Divide. How many 6s fit in 25? 4 (6 × 4 = 24; 6 × 5 = 30 is too big). Write 4 above the 5 in the tens place.
Multiply. 4 × 6 = 24. Write 24 under the 25.
Subtract. 25 − 24 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 6.

notes.say: Praise each step. When she says 1 is smaller than 6, cheer: "That check is how you never get a remainder that is too big."

slides.title: 853 ÷ 6: the ones
slides.text: One more round. Then look at what is left.

steps.text: Bring down. Bring down the 3 from the ones place. Now you have 13.
Divide. How many 6s fit in 13? 2 (6 × 2 = 12; 6 × 3 = 18 is too big). Write 2 above the 3 in the ones place.
Multiply. 2 × 6 = 12. Write 12 under the 13.
Subtract. 13 − 12 = 1. Check: 1 is smaller than 6. There are no more digits to bring down, so 853 ÷ 6 = 142 R 1.
Check: 142 × 6 = 852, and 852 + 1 = 853. It matches!

notes.do: She finishes on her paper and holds it up to the camera.
notes.ask: "Is 1 smaller than 6? Are there any digits left to bring down?" (Yes; no. So R 1.)

items.q: Fishlegs wrote 83 ÷ 9 = 8 R 11. The remainder is too big. Revise it. What is the right answer?
items.why: 11 is not smaller than 9, so one more 9 fits: 9 × 9 = 81, and 83 − 81 = 2. So 83 ÷ 9 = 9 R 2.
no: Check: 8 × 9 = 72, not 83. You cannot just drop a remainder.

items.q: 617 ÷ 3. The work is done. What is the remainder?
items.why: After the last subtraction, 2 is left, and 2 is smaller than 3. So 617 ÷ 3 = 205 R 2.
items.no: Look at the very last number, after the last subtraction.

notes.ask: On Fishlegs: "How do you know without dividing that it is wrong?" (11 is bigger than 9.)
notes.listen: 617 ÷ 3 has a placeholder 0 AND a remainder: 205 R 2. Praise her if she notices the 0.

items.q: A dragon refuses to come down from the roof, no matter what anyone says. The dragon is being…

items.q: The Vikings had ample fish for the feast. What does that mean?
choices: They had just a few fish.
They had more than enough fish.
items.why: Ample means more than enough.
no: Ample is the opposite of none.

questions.q: When you divide by 5, what is the biggest remainder you can ever have?
questions.why: The remainder must be smaller than the divisor, so the maximum remainder for ÷ 5 is 4. A remainder of 5 would make one more group.

questions.q: Every answer below checks out when you multiply back. Which one can not be right?
questions.why: In 31 ÷ 4 = 6 R 7, the remainder 7 is not smaller than 4, so another group fits. Revise it: 31 ÷ 4 = 7 R 3.
no: 3 is smaller than 5, so this remainder is allowed. Check: 9 × 5 + 3 = 48.
1 is smaller than 6, so this remainder is allowed. Check: 9 × 6 + 1 = 55.
1 is smaller than 9, so this remainder is allowed. Check: 9 × 9 + 1 = 82.

questions.why: 16 × 6 = 96, and 96 + 1 = 97. It matches the dividend, so the answer is right.
questions.no: Multiply 16 × 6 first. Then add the remainder 1.

questions.q: Fishlegs wrote 76 ÷ 9 = 7 R 13. The remainder is too big. Revise it. What is the right answer?
questions.why: 13 is not smaller than 9, so one more 9 fits: 8 × 9 = 72, and 76 − 72 = 4. So 76 ÷ 9 = 8 R 4.
no: Check: 7 × 9 = 63, not 76. You cannot just drop a remainder.

questions.q: Share 23 cookies among 4 friends. Each friend gets 5. The 3 cookies that remain are the ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
questions.why: The 3 cookies are the leftover: what remains after the sharing. In division, the leftover is the remainder.

questions.q: Which word means to change something to make it correct?
questions.why: To revise is to change something to make it correct.
no: Exceed means to be more than.
Ample means more than enough.
Maximum is the greatest amount allowed.

teacher.objective: Bailey does long division with remainders for 2- and 3-digit dividends ÷ 1-digit divisors (97 ÷ 4 = 24 R 1, 853 ÷ 6 = 142 R 1). She knows the remainder must be smaller than the divisor (the maximum remainder is the divisor minus 1), revises an answer whose remainder is too big, and checks every answer with quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.
materials: Zoom: share your screen with the Class lesson (teacher code 9110)
Whiteboard and marker (Jonathan), on camera, with the four steps, remainder < divisor, and the check rule
At Bailey's home (ask Tia to set out before the lesson): 9 dimes and about 40 pennies (or paper strips and beans), 6 paper plates
Paper and a pencil for Bailey; she holds her work up to the camera
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Packet (2 pages): printed later this week; it is assigned on Tuesday's task list

plan.do: Class slide 1. Coins, plates, paper and pencil at her table. Quick fact: 50 ÷ 8.
Class slide 2. What happened this weekend, Toothless being stubborn and Hiccup's response, does Hiccup give up.
Class slide 3. 4 × 4 = 16, 17 − 16 = 1, 45 ÷ 7 = 6 R 3; she says them, you type.
Class slide 4. She reads each card and makes her own sentence; remainder < divisor on your whiteboard.
Class slide 5. Dimes first, trade the extra dime, 17 pennies, 1 left: 24 R 1.
Class slides 6–7. She says each step before you click; praise each correct step.
Class slides 8–9. Multiply, then add the remainder; maximum remainder; revise Snotlout's 59 ÷ 7 = 7 R 10.
Class slide 10. Maximum for ÷ 6, which answer cannot be right, check 67 ÷ 5.
Class slides 11–13. Estimate between 100 and 200; she says each step; 142 R 1, check 852 + 1.
Class slide 14. 75 ÷ 4 and 589 ÷ 5; she leads, you praise each step.
Class slide 15. Fishlegs's 83 ÷ 9 = 8 R 11; the remainder of 617 ÷ 3.
Class slide 16. Stubborn, maximum, ample; revise and remnant in her own sentences.
Class slide 17. 86 ÷ 3, 749 ÷ 3 and a check, alone on paper.
Class slide 18. Course page: tonight the After-class lesson (needs 90) and 10 minutes of reading; Reading Power on Tuesday or Wednesday.

watch: A remainder as big as or bigger than the divisor (83 ÷ 9 = 8 R 11). Ask: "Could one more group of 9 fit?"
Forgetting to add the remainder when checking (24 × 4 = 96 and stopping). Point to the whiteboard rule: multiply, THEN add.
Writing the remainder as a digit in the quotient (97 ÷ 4 = 241). Ask: "Is there a digit up top for the 1 to sit over?" It goes after R.
A leftover in the middle step that is too big (in 853 ÷ 6, writing 3 for 25 ÷ 6 and leaving 7). Have her say "Is it smaller than 6?" after every subtraction.
Dropping a placeholder 0 when there is also a remainder (617 ÷ 3 = 25 R 2). Ask: "Estimate first: about 20 or about 200?"
"I can't do it." Ask only: "What is the first step?" When she does it, praise that one step out loud, then ask for the next.

packet_key.answer: leftover → what remains after the rest is shared out; exceed → to be more than; maximum → the greatest possible or allowed; revise → to change something to make it correct; remnant → a small piece of something bigger that is left; stubborn → not willing to change your mind; ample → more than enough
8 is bigger than 5, so one more group of 5 fits. 5 × 7 = 35 and 38 − 35 = 3: 38 ÷ 5 = 7 R 3.
Answers vary; a real moment from the book, stubborn used correctly, and Hiccup's response.
